chunks: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him):
'A man whose father invited him to accept appointment as executor of his will — is it permissible for him to refuse to accept the executorship?'
So he (peace be upon him) endorsed (in reply): 'It is not permissible for him to refuse.'

key_terms.وَصِيَّة: Wasiyya — a will or testament; also used for the appointment of a wasi (executor/guardian). In Islamic law, wasiyya can refer to both the document itself and the role of executor.
key_terms.وَقَّعَ: Waqqa'a — to endorse or sign a written response; in Shia hadith literature this verb often refers to the Imam's practice of responding to written questions by endorsing the query with a brief written reply (tawqi').
key_terms.يَمْتَنِعَ: Yamtani'a — to abstain or refuse; the legal question centers on whether refusal of the executorship role is permissible.

ai.seo_question: Can a son refuse to be executor of his father's will in Islam?
ai.summary: Ali ibn al-Rayyan wrote a question to Imam Abu al-Hasan (AS) asking whether a son may legally refuse when his father appoints him as executor (wasi) of his will. The Imam responded concisely by written endorsement (tawqi') that no, the son does not have the right to refuse. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that accepting executorship of a parent's will is a filial and legal obligation, rooted in respecting parental wishes and maintaining familial duties (sila al-rahim).
